Paper-individuality · segmentation · 19 Aug 2026

Is forepaw bias behaviour, or the camera?

Mice differ enormously and reproducibly in which forepaw they move more, and that difference predicts which way each animal turns the wheel. The group average bias, though, is pure instrument: lightningPose's own smoother strips 28% of real 8 Hz movement from a 60 fps recording and only 4% from a 150 fps one — and the bias reverses in the rigs wired the other way round.

00

Which paw is which, and can the two be compared at all?

Both side cameras label a paw_l and a paw_r, and the design-matrix pipeline takes paw_r from each camera and calls them l_paw and r_paw. That is only a left/right contrast if the two are genuinely different paws, so it was tested rather than assumed, on the 68 sessions with both cameras cached locally across 10 labs.

Left-camera paw_r correlates with right-camera paw_l at r = 0.64, but with right-camera paw_r at only r = 0.34 — in 64 of 68 sessions. The labels are image-space and the cameras are mirrored, so the two signals are different paws. Comparing each physical paw's scaled excursion between the two views then shows which camera sees it from close up: l_paw is the near view in 62 of 68 sessions, and so is r_paw.

Verdict

l_paw is the left forepaw and r_paw the right, both from the well-resolved near camera. The pipeline's naming is correct.

But the amplitudes are not comparable

get_speed divides left-camera pixels by two, because that camera is 1280×1024 against the right camera's 640×512. That correctly equates spatial scale — and simultaneously halves the left camera's tracking noise while leaving the right camera's at full size.

Every measure of measurement error is roughly twice as large on the right paw.
Noise measureLeft pawRight pawRatio
High-frequency jitter residual1.67 px3.16 px1.95×
Per-paw SNR, P(0.5–8 Hz) / P(32 Hz)133512.6×
32 Hz power — a forepaw cannot oscillate this fast, so this band is nearly all errorLI = −0.48right-shifted

The consequence is severe. The raw amplitude index correlates r = +0.80 with the 32 Hz noise index, and on unfiltered frame-to-frame speed the right paw looks about twice as fast in nearly every session. The spectral signature seals it: the left/right difference grows monotonically with frequency and flips sign at ~4 Hz — precisely what a flat additive noise floor on one side produces, because noise dominates wherever real movement power is lowest.

Read this before any group mean

No population-level left/right paw preference can be claimed from this dataset. The group means below are reported for completeness and are instrumental, not biological.

But which artefact? Sections 04 and 05 test this directly, and the answer is not the noise floor described here — it is a multiplicative camera gain error. The noise floor turns out to contaminate only speed-type measures, not the 0.5–8 Hz band the clustering uses. Read section 04 before acting on anything in this section.

01

Paw bias is a strong, stable property of the individual mouse

ICC(1) with sessions nested in mice (76 mice, 307 sessions). The permutation null — shuffling session→mouse — has a 95th percentile near 0.08 for every metric, so all rows sit far outside chance at p_perm = 1×10⁻⁴.
MetricICCContamination (r with 32 Hz noise)
LI amplitude, 0.5–8 Hz power0.815+0.80
LI SNR — gain-invariant0.845−0.14
Bilateral coupling (peak cross-correlation)0.790−0.19
LI bout rate at matched duty cycle0.512−0.23
Lead–lag: which paw leads0.453−0.21
LI jitter — the artefact itself0.824+0.92

Four independent lines of support:

  • Across-session reliability is r = 0.867, against a within-session split-half ceiling of r = 0.889. A mouse's paw bias reproduces between two sessions about as well as between two halves of one session — it is essentially noise-free at session level.
  • 55% of the 58 mice with ≥3 sessions have every single session on the same side of the population median (chance 13%, p_perm = 1×10⁻⁴).
  • It is not a lab effect. Between-lab differences are significant by session but vanish once each mouse counts once (F = 0.73, p = 0.69). Centring each metric within its own lab still leaves ICC = 0.789.
  • The scale-free metrics are only weakly noise-contaminated and remain highly significant, so the individuality is not purely instrumental.
The limitation that this dataset cannot settle

The jitter index is itself mouse-stable, at ICC = 0.824. Each mouse is typically recorded on a single rig with fixed camera geometry, so a stable per-animal difference in how that mouse sits relative to the two cameras is indistinguishable from behavioural individuality here.

Treat the raw amplitude ICC of 0.815 as an upper bound, and lean on the gain-invariant and scale-free metrics for claims. Settling it properly needs a within-rig manipulation, or the same mouse recorded on two rigs.

02

What survives predicts which way the mouse turns the wheel

Both sign conventions were checked against the data rather than taken from documentation: choice == −1 is the right-side report (it occurs on 94.6% of high-contrast right-stimulus trials, matching the 94.6% accuracy there), and positive wheel velocity is what produces it (mean +1.1 versus −1.2 in the 300 ms after first movement). The two correlations therefore point the same way, which is a real consistency check rather than a restatement.

Mice that use their left paw relatively more also turn the wheel further in the report-right direction, and make more right-side choices — including at 0% contrast, where there is no correct answer. Paw-usage bias and choice-side bias are two faces of one individual asymmetry.

Nothing predicts task performance. The noise index is itself weakly related to wheel bias (r = +0.23, p = 0.021), which is exactly why the claim rests on the partial correlation and the gain-invariant SNR version — both survive.

03

Bilateral coordination is a separate individual trait

The peak cross-correlation between the two paw speed traces is 0.49 ± 0.10 across mice, with ICC = 0.790: how tightly an animal couples its two forepaws is a strong, stable individual property, and it is a correlation, so per-paw gain errors cannot manufacture it. It is unrelated to performance (r = −0.035).

Mean lead–lag is essentially zero (−4 ms, p = 0.23), but it is mouse-specific (ICC = 0.453; 55% of mice sign-consistent against 24.5% chance). Which paw leads is idiosyncratic rather than shared across the population.

04

Tested: does degrading the left camera fix it?

Real downsampling would mean re-encoding the video at 640×512 and re-running lightningPose, which cannot be done post-hoc. Two surrogates bracket what it would do, run on 213 sessions from the 58 mice with three or more sessions, alongside the whitening alternative:

  • QUANT — snap left-paw coordinates onto the right camera's pixel grid. The floor of the effect: sub-pixel precision only.
  • MATCH — add Gaussian positional noise to the left paw, calibrated per session so its 32 Hz power equals the right paw's. The full effect, with the calibration verified rather than assumed.
  • WHITEN — divide each paw's 0.5–8 Hz bands by its own 32 Hz band.
Criteria were fixed before running the test. MATCH equalises the noise floors — and changes nothing that matters.
CriterionRAWQUANTMATCHWHITEN
C1  LI[32 Hz] → 0−0.403−0.125+0.014 ✓0 by construction
C2  r(LI[band power], noise) → 0+0.771+0.771+0.767−0.125
C3  per-frequency slope−0.030/oct−0.027−0.025—
C4  between-mouse ICC0.8290.8290.8270.791
C5  LI × wheel bias+0.432+0.434+0.432+0.148, p=0.26

MATCH does equalise the noise floors — and it moves the metric the clustering uses by nothing at all: LI[0.5–8 Hz power] correlates r = 0.9999 between RAW and MATCH. The speed index, by contrast, moves a great deal (r = 0.79, mean flipping sign from −0.107 to +0.048).

There is a clean analytic reason. The wavelets run on velocity, i.e. differenced position, and differencing shapes white tracking noise into a high-pass spectrum, |H(f)|² ∝ sin²(πf/fs):

Noise power that white positional error contributes to each velocity band, relative to the 32 Hz band.
Band0.5 Hz1 Hz2 Hz4 Hz8 Hz32 Hz
Relative noise power0.07%0.28%1.1%4.4%16.7%100%

The 32 Hz channel is roughly 90× more noise-sensitive than the 2 Hz channel. The noise floor dominates exactly where it was detected, and is nearly absent where the clustering actually lives.

This corrects an earlier conclusion in this report

The r = +0.80 correlation between the raw amplitude index and the 32 Hz noise index was read as causal contamination of the 0.5–8 Hz band. It is not: equalising the noise leaves that correlation at +0.767 and leaves the metric at r = 0.9999 of itself. The correlation reflects a shared cause — per-mouse and per-rig camera geometry driving both indices — not contamination.

Downsampling the left camera is therefore the wrong fix, and whitening is actively harmful: it swings the index from −0.14 to +0.26 and destroys the wheel-bias correlation (p = 0.26), because the divisor is itself asymmetric.

05

What the group-level bias actually is: a frame-rate artefact

Each side camera tracks both paws, which allows laterality to be measured within a single camera — never comparing across the two, so no cross-camera gain can enter. Using the paw identities established in section 00:

  • LI_leftcam = LI( leftcam paw_r [left paw, near], leftcam paw_l [right paw, far] )
  • LI_rightcam = LI( rightcam paw_l [left paw, far], rightcam paw_r [right paw, near] )

Each is still biased by near-versus-far foreshortening, but in opposite directions, because the left paw is the near one in the left camera and the far one in the right. Writing the four log band-powers in terms of true laterality τ, foreshortening f and camera gain γ gives an exactly-determined system — four log-amplitudes yield three independent contrasts — solved on the 68 two-camera sessions (41 mice, 10 labs).

Decomposition on 68 sessions with both cameras cached. Identification assumes the foreshortening factor is common to the two cameras, which the rig's mirror symmetry makes reasonable.
TermEstimateEvidence
τ  true laterality+0.027, p = 0.3638/68 positive — no population preference
f  near/far foreshortening+0.13966/68 positive, p = 2e−25
γ  camera gain+0.08957/68 positive, p = 2e−11
pipeline index (τ − γ)−0.062p = 0.047

The direct evidence is a double dissociation. The same two physical paws, measured by the swapped cameras, give LI = +0.116 where the pipeline's pairing gives −0.062. Swap which camera measures which paw and the sign flips — so the group-level bias is about the cameras, not the paws.

γ = +0.089 corresponds to the left camera reading about 16% low overall. But γ turns out not to be a spatial scale error at all, and no constant can fix it.

The spatial correction is already right

Whether the left camera really has twice the linear resolution is measurable directly, from landmarks both cameras see — above all the lick tube, rig hardware of fixed physical size, which needs no assumption about the mouse.

Three independent references, 68 sessions. The ÷2 assumption survives; the 1.675 implied by the paw analysis does not.

The rig is spatially symmetric and the ÷2 is correct.

γ is temporal: it comes from the frame-rate asymmetry

A spatial gain error would be flat across frequency. γ is not — it grows steeply, from a 0.93 amplitude ratio at 0.5 Hz to 0.72 at 8 Hz (paired 8 Hz vs 0.5 Hz, t = +10.0, p = 5e−15).

The cause is the frame rate, not the side. The left camera usually runs at 60 fps and the right at 150 fps, and the slower camera under-measures fast movement twice over: a longer exposure (up to ~16.7 ms against ≤6.7 ms) blurs a moving paw toward the middle of its excursion, and coarser temporal sampling followed by linear interpolation onto the 60 Hz analysis grid — a triangular kernel one full sample wide — attenuates it further. The pipeline compounds this by low-pass filtering only the faster camera.

The decisive evidence: in the five rigs where the LEFT camera is the fast one, the bias reverses sign.
Rig configurationnγ @ 0.5 Hzγ @ 8 Hz
left 60 Hz, right 150 Hz61+0.037+0.192
left 150 Hz, right 60 Hz5−0.006−0.047

γ at 8 Hz correlates with log₂(right_fr / left_fr) at r = +0.56 (p = 7e−7); γ at 0.5 Hz does not (r = 0.10, p = 0.43). And τ stays non-significant at every frequency (+0.009 to +0.033, all p > 0.3) — there is no population paw preference at any timescale.

Correction to an earlier version of this report

An earlier version recommended setting RESOLUTION['left'] ≈ 2.39. That was wrong twice over: the value was inverted, so it would have doubled the bias rather than removing it, and the whole approach aimed at the wrong dimension. The problem is temporal, so no constant spatial factor can fix it.

Where the attenuation originates — and why the resampling code cannot fix it

The 30 Hz anti-alias filter is not the culprit: at 150 Hz sampling a 4th-order 30 Hz Butterworth has gain 0.999996 at 8 Hz and 1.000000 below 4 Hz, so it is transparent in the clustering band. It is also correct — resampling 150 → 60 Hz requires anti-aliasing below the 30 Hz Nyquist — and it is applied on if fr > 60, i.e. to whichever camera is fast, not to a fixed side.

Processing genuinely-150 Hz traces as if they had come from a 60 fps camera (box-average over 1/60 s to model the longer exposure, decimate, then the same route) bounds what exposure and sampling can account for.

19 sessions with a genuine 150 Hz camera. Exposure and sampling explain a third of the penalty at 8 Hz and none of it at low frequency.

The remainder arises before the design matrix, in lightningPose itself — plausibly its ensemble-Kalman post-processing, which would smooth over a longer real-time window at a lower frame rate, though that is not verified here.

Two further corrections

Earlier versions of this report recommended (a) not low-pass filtering only one camera, and (b) box-averaging the fast camera to match the slow one. Both are withdrawn: the filter is transparent in the band and is correct anti-aliasing applied by frame rate rather than by side, and the box-average recovers only about a third of the penalty at 8 Hz and none at low frequency.

The mechanism, measured

The pose files carry two versions of every keypoint: <kp>_ens_median, the median across the ensemble of networks with no temporal smoothing, and <kp>_x, the output of lightningPose's ensemble Kalman smoother. The ratio of their velocity spectra is the smoother's transfer function — measurable at each camera's native rate, entirely independent of the design matrix.

The smoother strips 28% of real 8 Hz movement from a 60 fps recording and only 4% from a 150 fps one.

4 Hz0.8890.9730.9140.84154%
8 Hz0.7180.9560.7500.68178%

That is consistent with the smoother's time constant being set per frame rather than per second, so at 60 fps it smooths over a 2.5× longer real-time window. In the five reversed rigs the roles swap, as they must if this is causal: the left/right ratio becomes 1.025 instead of 0.750.

Stacking the two independently measured stages accounts for the frequency-dependent part almost exactly, and leaves a flat residual.

So γ has exactly two components. The frequency-dependent one is solved: the smoother dominates (78% at 8 Hz), exposure and resampling follow (31%), and together they predict 0.676 against 0.681 observed. The frequency-flat ~7% deficit remains open — the residual is 0.929 ± 0.009 across 0.5–4 Hz, strikingly constant, and it is none of the smoother, resampling, exposure, the anti-alias filter, or tracking noise, all of which are measured and excluded.

The remaining candidates, in order: depth perspective — the scale references (tube, pupil, nose) all sit at the midline or head while the near paw is much closer to the lens, so slightly different working distances would shift px/mm at the paw's depth while matching at the head, frequency-flat by construction and invisible to the landmark test; residual scale error — the measured ratios were 1.980 / 1.986 / 1.954, and a true value near 1.96 is worth about a quarter of the effect; and estimator leakage — the decomposition assumes near/far foreshortening is identical in both cameras, and if it is not, part of this residual is really asymmetric f, which would give τ a small bias too. Note also that γ's session-to-session spread (0.092) exceeds its mean (0.089) and only 22% of its variance is between-lab, so most of γ is session-level — pointing at how the mouse sits on a given day rather than at fixed hardware.

What to do instead

  • Build the design matrix from the _ens_median columns rather than the smoothed ones. The smoother is the single largest contributor to the bias, and it removes nothing needed here: the noise it suppresses is high-frequency, and the MATCH test already established that the 32 Hz noise floor does not affect the 0.5–8 Hz clustering band (r = 0.9999). This should remove ~78% of the 8 Hz bias at no real cost, and it is directly testable by re-running gamma_spectrum.py on those traces.
  • For any laterality claim — use the within-camera estimator. Both paws from a single camera cancels γ exactly, whatever the residual cause, with no correction constant.
  • Cheapest — keep features at ≤2 Hz, where the total penalty is ~7% rather than 32%, at the cost of the fast bands the lateralised states rely on.
  • Do not change the resampling or filtering code. It contributes little and the filter is correct anti-aliasing.

What this does not change

Everything in sections 01–03 survives, because γ is uncorrelated with τ (r = 0.035, p = 0.77) and so acts as an additive offset rather than a driver of individual variation. The between-mouse ICC goes 0.829 → 0.827 under MATCH; the pipeline index tracks the camera-free laterality estimate at r = 0.931; and the wheel-bias correlation is unchanged at r = +0.432 (p = 0.0003). The individuality and the choice-side link are real — only the group mean was an artefact.

06

Method notes and caveats

  • All laterality indices are LI = (left − right) / (left + right), so positive means left paw.
  • Positions are low-passed at a common 8 Hz before differentiating, so the two paws receive identical noise treatment; the primary amplitude measure is 0.5–8 Hz wavelet band power rather than frame-difference speed.
  • Tracking NaNs are dropped, never interpolated. Lead–lag and bout statistics run on NaN-dropped traces, so bins adjacent to camera dropouts contribute small edge artefacts (NaN fraction is typically 0–4%).
  • LI[bout duration] is exactly −LI[bout rate] at matched duty cycle; only one carries information.
  • Session exclusions are kept in sync with those in 3.3_wavelet_clusters.ipynb. That notebook is not modified by this analysis.
  • The Morlet transform used in sections 04–05 is a vectorised rewrite of segmentation_functions.fast_wavelet_morlet_convolution_parallel, verified equal to 5×10⁻¹⁵ relative; the original calls joblib Parallel(n_jobs=-1) per invocation, which oversubscribes badly inside a process pool.
  • The τ / f / γ decomposition is exactly determined, not over-determined — the four log band-powers give only three independent contrasts, so the two ways of writing τ are algebraically identical and their agreement is not independent corroboration.
